Langston Hughes. The poet, writer, and cultural innovator central to the Harlem Renaissance, known for infusing his poetry with jazz rhythms, blues idiom, and vernacular speech. His work celebrated Black culture while critiquing American racism, and his prolific output made him one of the most influential voices of twentieth-century American letters.

Hughes pioneered jazz poetry, incorporating the rhythms and improvisational spirit of jazz music into verse, making formal poetry accessible to Black audiences. His debut collection, The Weary Blues, published in 1926, brought Harlem nightlife, blues feeling, and African-American voice to literary prominence. The poem Harlem, published in 1951, asks the unforgettable question: What happens to a dream deferred? This stark, memorable exploration of delayed Black aspiration became canonical in American letters.

His short stories, collected in works like The Ways of White Folks, examined racism and racial hypocrisy with wit and moral clarity. Across a fifty-year career, Hughes wrote plays, translations, children's literature, essays, and journalism, making him a cultural polymath. Importantly, he centered Black joy, resilience, and dignity alongside critique of oppression, refusing a purely victimological framing of Black life. His influence extended through Gwendolyn Brooks, who built on his foundation of bringing vernacular speech and jazz into poetry, and through Maya Angelou and others who adopted his example of using verse for social witness.
